Cutting down power losses 
1511. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
 SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: 
 SHRI JESUDASU SEELAM: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has taken serious steps and made efforts to cut 
down losses of power in the country; 
(b) whether the power losses and theft currently form 20- 24 per cent 
of overall average; 
(c) if so, whether the need to bring down these losses is an urgent 
economic imperative; 
(d) whether the Ministry has taken various steps in this regard and 
had called a meeting of all concerned; and 
(e) if so, what are the main decisions taken and what are the steps 
being considered to improve the position? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): 
(a) to (d) The draft report on Performance of State Power Utilities for 
the years 2004- 05 to 2006- 07 prepared by the Power Finance Corporation 
indicates that the Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) Loss of the 
State Power Utilities at the national level for 2006-07 was 33.07% of the 
total energy available for sale. 
Govt. of India had launched the flagship programme viz. Accelerated 
Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP) in 2002- 03 with the 
objective of encouraging reforms, reducing Aggregate Technical and 
Commercial (AT&C) loss, improving quality of supply of power and 
improving consumer satisfaction in the X Plan. The target was to reduce 
AT&C losses to 15% in five years to begin with in urban and high density 
consumption areas. AT&C loss has come down in towns where APDRP has been 
implemented. Further, some of the utilities which adopted various 

283 
interventions as envisaged under the programme have shown significant 
reduction in AT&C loss. Under the programme, 571 projects were sanctioned 
covering approx. 906 towns in the country. At town level, AT&C losses 
have been brought below 20 percent in 215 APDRP towns in the country of 
which 163 towns have brought AT&C losses below 15 percent. However, 
according to draft report on Performance of State Power Utilities 
prepared by the Power Finance Corporation, the national AT&C loss levels 
were brought down from 36.64% in 2002-03 to 33.07% in 2006-07. 

284 
The Central Government has built a national consensus to focus on a 
time bound programme for reduction of AT&C losses. In the Chief 
Ministers' Conference held under the C hairmanship of the Prime Minister 
on 28th May 2007, a unanimous resolution was adopted which inter alia  
included the commitment of the States, with appropriate assistance from 
the Centre, to establish the necessary baseline data and information 
technology applications for energy accounting and auditing, and for 
ensuring a resolute elimination of electricity theft. 
(e) The Government have approved the continuation of APDRP during the 
XI Five Year Plan with revised terms and conditions as a Central Sector 
Scheme. The focus of the programme during XI Plan is on actual, 
demonstrable performance in terms of loss reduction. In the project area, 
the State Power Utilities are expected to achieve Aggregate Technical & 
Commercial (AT&C) loss reduction target of 15%. The Utilities are also to 
achieve the following target of AT&C loss reduction at utility level: 
• Utilities having AT&C loss above 30%: Reduction by 3% per year 
• Utilities having AT&C loss below 30%: Reduction by 1.5% per year 
Projects under the scheme are to be taken up in Two Parts. Part- A is 
to include the projects for establishment of baseline data and IT 
applications for energy accounting / auditing & IT based consumer service 
centers. Part- B includes regular distribution strengthening projects. 
Scheme also contains provision of incentive for utility staff in towns 
where AT&C loss levels are brought below the base line levels. 
Changes in power sector 
1512. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: 
 SHRI VIJAY JAWAHARLAL DARDA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the country's power sector needs radical changes 
particularly in distribution sector; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the generation and distribution of power is not upto the 
mark resulting in affecting the economic growth; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government proposes to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): 
(a) to (d) Government of India is well aware of the needs of the power 
sector in the present dynamic scenario. Government of India has enacted 
Electricity Act 2003 and launched a number of important programmes like 
the Accelerated Power Development and Reforms Programme (APDRP), Rajiv 
Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY), Capacity Addition Programme, 
Development of National Grid and the Energy Efficiency and Conservation 
Programme, etc. for improving the power sector of the country. 

285 
Radical changes, particularly in distribution sector have already been 
mandated in the Electricity Act 2003, as under:- 
 i) Restructuring of State Electricity Board. 
 (ii) Endeavour to extend supply to all villages/ hamlets. 

286 
 (iii) No requirement of license for generation and if a person 
intends to generate and distribute power in rural area, no licence 
is required. 
 (vi) Distribution to be licensed by State Electricity Regulatory 
Commissions (SERCs). 
 (v) Distribution licenses free to take up generation and generation 
company free to take up distribution license. This would 
facilitate private sector participation without Government 
guarantee/ escrow. 
 (vi) Retail tariff to be determined by the Regulatory Commission. 
 (vii) Metering made compulsory. 
 (viii) Open access in distribution to be allowed by SERC in 
phases. 
 (ix) Stringent provisions for theft of electricity. 
 (x) Measures for protection of consumer interest. 
An important programme of Capacity Addition in the generation sector 
has been worked out by Ministry of Power. National Electricity Policy 
envisages "Power for all by 2012" and per capita availability of power to 
be increased to over 1000 units by 2011- 12. Under the Electricity Act, 
2003, the setting up of generation capacity has been substantially 
liberalized. The Ministry has in consultation with the Planning 
Commission fixed a target of adding 78,760 MW in the XI Plan. Based on 
the present status of ongoing generation projects, the Central 
Electricity Authority (CEA) has estimated that a larger generation 
capacity of 79790 MW could be feasible from conventional sources during 
the 11th Plan. A capacity of 11322 MW has already been added and 68468 MW 
is under construction. 
Another major program of the Ministry of Power is the development of 
the national grid, nearly 17,000 MW inter- regional power transfer 
capacity has been established to transmit bulk power at extra high 
voltage from resource rich areas to deficit areas across the country. 
The APDRP was launched in 2002- 03 with the-  objective of encouraging 
State level reforms, reducing Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) 
losses, improving the quality of supply of power and improving consumer 
satisfaction. Under the programme, 571 projects were sanctioned covering 
approximately 906 towns in the country. At the town level, AT&C losses 
have been brought below 20 per cent in 215 APDRP towns in the country, of 
which 163 towns have brought AT&C losses below 1 5 per cent. Keeping in 
mind the suggestions of the various stakeholders, the focus of recently 
approved restructured APDRP in XI Plan is on actual, demonstrable 
performance in terms of loss reduction. In the project areas, the State 
Power Utilities are expected to reduce AT&C losses to 15%. The Utilities 
are also to achieve the following target of AT&C loss reduction for the 
utility as a whole: 
• Utilities having AT&C loss above 30%: Reduction by 3% per year 

287 
• Utilities having AT&C loss below 30%: Reduction by 1.5% per year 
Projects under the scheme are to be taken up in Two Parts. Part- A is 
to include the projects for establishment of baseline data and use of 
information technology (IT) applications for energy accounting / auditing 
and setting up of IT based consumer service centers. Part- B includes 
regular distribution strengthening projects. 

288 
Under the Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran Yojana (RGGVY), as on 
date, 558 projects have been sanctioned with an outlay of Rs. 25,679.64 
crore for providing electricity to 1,16,124 un -electrified villages, 
intensive electrification of 3,49,853 already electrified villages, 
releasing electricity connections to 4.09 crore rural households 
including 2.43 crore Below Poverty Line (BPL) households. The cumulative 
achievement is the electrification of 53,048 hitherto un- electrified 
villages, intensive electrification of 66,808 already electrified 
villages and provision of electricity connections to 48.18 lakh rural 
households including 40.76 lakh BPL households. 
In order to manage and boost energy efficiency, the Ministry is 
implementing a programme to encourage greater energy efficiency in the 
use of electricity laying down standards for minimum energy performance 
for electrical equipment and new commercial buildings, to promote 
agricultural and municipal demand side management, promote energy 
efficiency in small and medium enterprises and operationalise the Energy 
Conservation Act, 2001 by strengthening state designated agencies. The 
targeted reduction in demand by these interventions has been kept at 5% 
of the total capacity at the end of XI Plan, which translates into an 
avoided capacity addition of 10000 MW.

Problems in power sector 
†1517. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: 
   SHRI BRIJ BHUSHAN TIWARI: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the power generation is not in 
proportion to its consumption, as a result of which the people are facing 
the problem of low frequency and tripping; 
(b) if so, whether Government is formulating any effective plan to 
increase power generation and whether Government intends to formulate any 
plan to give boost to solar energy; 
(c) whether transmission losses also are one of the reasons for power 
problem; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): 
(a) The rate of growth of demand for power is outstripping the growth in 
its availability, the power generation in the country falls short of the 
total requirement. Low frequency is experienced in power system whenever 
the connected load becomes more than the available generation. In order 
to maintain safety and security of the grid, load shedding is also 
resorted to in various S tates /systems from time to time, by 
disconnection of supply feeders, manually and also through automatic 
under-frequency operation, commensurate with the availability of power. 
(b) In order to meet increasing demand of power, Government has set a 
Capacity Addition target of 78,700 MW from utility power plants during 
the 11th Five Year Plan. On the basis of latest assessment, capacity 
addition of 79,790 MW is feasible during the 11th Plan, out of which 
11,322 MW has already been commissioned upto 30th November, 2008 and 
balance capacity of 68,468 MW is under construction. 
The other measures taken/being taken to improve power generation in 
the country include close monitoring and review of capacity addition of 
the on-going power generation projects, development of a number of Ultra 
Mega Power Projects of 4000 MW each under competitive bidding, harnessing 
surplus captive power into grid, import of coal to bridge the gap between 
domestic availability of coal and anticipated demand of coal, etc. 

295 
A capacity addition of 15,000 MW (14,000 MW grid-interactive and 1,000 
MW off- grid /distributed) from renewable energy sources is envisaged 
during the 11th Plan. Thus, by the end of the 11th Plan grid- interactive 
renewable power installed capacity is likely to cross 24,000 MW or about 
11 per cent of the then likely total installed power generation capacity. 
A total outlay of Rs. 1,000 crore has been allocated for grid- interactive 
and distributed renewable power generation during the 11th Plan period. 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 

296 
The National Action Plan on Climate Change has identified large- scale 
solar power generation as one of the thrust areas under the Solar 
Mission. It envisages solar power capacity of 20,000 MW by 2020. 
(c) and (d) High Aggregate Technical and Commercial (AT&C) losses is 
one of the reasons contributing to power problem. While technical losses 
reduce the availability of power to the ultimate consumer, the commercial 
losses result in poor financial health of the distribution company. The 
draft report on Performance of State Power Utilities for the years 2004-
05 to 2006- 07 prepared by the Power Finance Corporation indicates that 
out of the total energy available for sale, the AT&C losses of the State 
Power Utilities at the national level for 2004- 05, 2005-06 and 2006- 07 
were 34.33 %, 34.54% and 32.07% respectively.

1522. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government has recently undertaken a detailed analysis of 
the commissioning schedule of various power projects across the country; 
(b) if so, the results thereof;

Ministry to change the definition of commissioning of power project to 
reflect its true operationalisation, as. nearly half of the new thermal 
power plants declared commissioned, during 2007- 08 are actually yet to 
get fully operational on commercial basis; and

various on-going power projects in  

306 
the country vis- a-vis their commissioning schedule. There is a well 
established mechanism for monitoring and review of these projects and 
also for initiating corrective measures wherever necessary to ensure that 
the projects are commissioned according to their schedule. Some of the 
important measures taken are as follows: 
• The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has appointed designated nodal 
officers to be associated with each on-going project, who continuously 
and closely monitor the progress at site through frequent visits and

rural, urban and tribal projects. 
The main findings of the appraisal are as under: 
• Around 59 per cent AWCs studied have no toilet facility and in 17 AWCs 
this facility was found to be unsatisfactory; 
• Around 75% of AWCs have pucca buildings; 
• 44 per cent AWCs covered under the study were found to be lacking PSE 
kits; 
• disruption of supplementary nutrition was noticed on an average of

reported as delay in supply of items of supplementary nutrition; 
• 36.5 per cent mothers did not report weighing of new born children;

respiratory infection sepsis, diarrhea and measles, low birth weight,

nutrition from Re. 1 to Rs. 21/- per beneficiary per day. 
– From the year 2005- 06, 50% cost of supplementary nutrition is also

Serious Flood situation in Tamil Nadu 
SHRI D. RAJA (Tamil Nadu): Thank you, Madam. Recently a cyclone called 
'Nisha' hit the coast of Tamil Nadu. It caused heavy rains and floods. 
Eleven districts of Tamil Nadu have been terribly  

395 
affected. The rice bowl of Tamil Nadu, which consists of several 
districts like Thanjavur, Thiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Cuddalore, is the 
worst hit. The loss of property and the loss of standing crop are 
estimated to the tune of more than Rs.8,000 crore. Over two crore people 
have been affected. The official figure says that 189 persons were killed 
due to floods and heavy rain. Farmers, fishermen, and agricultural 
workers are the people who have been terribly affected by the floods and 
heavy rain. About 4,997 cattle were killed. Even 1,597 villages are still 
under water today. The Government figures says that 5,06,675 huts or 
dwellings were totally destroyed and 4,93,970 huts were partially 
destroyed. 
The State Government has taken some relief measures, but they are not 
adequate. The central team which visited Tamil Nadu has acknowledged the 
devastation but yet to make a detailed assessment and proposals. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Union Government to extend more financial help 
to the State of Tamil Nadu. 
On the basis of the Calamity Relief Fund, the Centre says that it can 
only give Rs.4,000 per hectare as compensation. The State Government of 
the day, today, has announced another Rs.3,500. It makes the total amount 
of Rs.7,500 per hectare. There is a genuine demand from farmers and from 
many political organisations that the compensation should be from 
Rs.25,000 to Rs.35,000 per hectare. And this should be given as a relief. 
The Government should also think of launching a Comprehensive Crop 
Insurance Scheme. It is high time the Government came out with concrete 
proposals for comprehensive crop insurance. 
The houses constructed under the Indira Awas Yojana are the worst 
affected, during these floods and heavy rain. Only Rs.1,000 is given as 
compensation. It is nothing. Under the Indira Awas Yojana, only Rs.55,000 
were given for construction of houses. It is time the Government should 
think of constructing proper houses under this Scheme. This Scheme is 
meant for aam aadmi, the poor people. The poor people are dalits, 
agricultural workers, and fishermen in the country. This Scheme should be 
taken up with more sensitivity. 
Finally, Madam, the recommendations of the National Commission on 
Farmers headed by our distinguished colleague, Prof. M.S. Swaminathan, 
should be given due consideration. How long can it be kept pending? I do 
not understand it. We have seen floods in Bihar. We have seen floods in 
Assam. We have seen floods in Orissa. Now we are seeing floods in Tamil 
Nadu. ...(Interruptions)...

Demand to clear pending cases of pension to freedom fighters of Goa 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Madam, Goa is celebrating its 47th 
year of independence on 19th December 2008. We became liberated after 450 
years of Portuguese rule. But, Madam, unfortunately, hundreds of cases of 
freedom fighters from Goa are pending in the Home Ministry and they are 
being scrutinised at very slow pace. It is possible that scrutiny of 
documents can take time. But, Madam, it is seen that after an application 
is made, some officers will apply their mind, after about a year or so, 
to the application. Thereafter, in writing to the freedom fighter, they 
will take another one year. If a clarification is issued, to examine that 
clarification or requiring additional documents, they take another few 
months. In such a manner, Madam, it takes years together to scrutinise a 
simple application regarding freedom fighters. 
Now, Madam, in the present circumstances, when we have got the 
electronic medium, there is a way out that if any document is not 
missing, the State Government can be contacted and the State Government 
can, in turn, contact the concerned freedom fighter and obtain the 
necessary information and thereafter, the documents can be examined  and 
the information can be scrutinised and speedy justice can be given to the 
freedom fighters. Second option, Madam, is this that Lok Adalats can be 
held in all the States wherever applications of freedom fighters are 
pending and the officer concerned can come for 2- 3 days in the State 
Capitals or if there are many applications, in some districts and can 
call the freedom fighters, have interaction with them, find out the 
documents which are lacking, take information from them and dispose of 
the matter. In case some applications are remaining where documents 
required need time, then, they can be given further time and they can go 

400 
to the State Capitals and the documents can be sent. In this manner, 
disposal of freedom fighters' applications can be done speedily. 
Therefore, Madam, I request the Home Ministry to establish Lok Adalats 
for the disposal of freedom fighters cases from Goa.

effective laws.

workers. It will also help in enhancing the quality of tea in the 
international market.

Concern over findings of R.C. Bhargava Committee 
SHRI BHARATKUMAR RAUT (Maharashtra): Madam, I wish to attract the 
attention of the House to the Report of the R.C. Bhargava Committee, 
appointed by the HRD Ministry to look into the problems of admissions in 
the Indian Institutes of Management (IMs). 
The observations of the Committee are revealing. I am told that the 
Committee feels that the IIMs have not been fair to every meritorious 
candidate. High fees and different scholarship rules for different IIMs 
have kept deserving students out of the institutions. 
It is indeed a matter of shame that deserving students are deprived of 
education in these institutions only because they can't afford the huge 
amount of fees. On the one hand, we talk of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and, on 
the other, leave meritorious and desiring students out. If this is 
happening, it amounts to defeat of the basic purpose of giving strength 
to IIMs. 
As the private and public sector enterprises are on the rise in India 
and elsewhere, the need for more trained managers is also growing. In 
this situation, IIMs should allow more students from middle class and 
lower middle class to take admission. Otherwise, the IIMs will continue 
to remain a "reserved territory" for the haves, and the have- nots will 
remain out. 
My request is that the HRD Ministry should have a multi- level fee 
structure so that those having lower income can also come in. The system 
of scholarships also needs to be looked into afresh. The HRD Ministry can 
have more need- based loan scholarships or low interest loan schemes to 
achieve the principle of inclusive growth. Thank you.

Concern over shortage of vaccines for Universal Immunisation  
Programme in the country 
SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT (West Bengal): Madam, my Special Mention relates 
to a serious matter, the shortage of vaccines, which has arisen in the 
Universal Immunisation Programme. The decision of the Health Ministry to 
close down production in three public sector units of vaccines for the 
Universal Immunisation Programme has had the most serious consequences. 
There are significant shortages of vaccines in various States. For 
example, as on 27- 10-2008, West Bengal faced a shortage of vaccines TT 
68.69 per cent, BCG-12.45 per cent, DPT-88.49 per cent, Hepatitis-B-63.64 
per cent, Measles- 43.88 per cent, DT-  99.75 per cent. There was no DT 
available at all. In the first week of November additional 3 lakh doses 
of DPT were supplied, but the requirement was 1.33 crore doses. In 
Tripura, the annual requirement of six antigens is 3.80 lakh doses, but 
the total quantity received was only 1.25 lakh doses, a shortage of 67.11 
per cent. Against the requirement of 93,000 doses of DPT, the State had 
received not a single dose till 31st October. In Orissa, short supply 
against the total requirement is, DPT -  80.63 per cent, measles -  66.98 
per cent. In the case of DT, not even a single dose has been provided. In 
Kerala, the short supply against the total requirement of last seven 
months, including buffer stock is, BCG - 15.31 per cent, DPT - 40.53 per 
cent and in the case of DT, it is as high as 88.42 per cent. 

409 
The information given to the House by the Minister on 21.10.2008 was 
factually incorrect. The Minister had assured the House that there were 
only one or two instances of shortages, which were not gross shortages 
and the issues have been sorted out. The shortage still continues and it 
concerns a range of vaccines. It will be in the national interest if the 
Government gives immediate permission for production of low cost and safe 
vaccines in the three PSUs.

Demand to reduce the prices of petrol and diesel 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN (West Bengal): Madam, it is unfortunate that the 
Government is refusing to reduce the prices of petrol and diesel despite 
a steady fall in the international oil prices. The international oil 
prices had fallen below 42 dollars per barrel in the mid- November, 2008. 
The administered price of petrol and diesel was increased in June, 2008, 
by Rs.5 and Rs.3 per litre of petrol and diesel when the international 
oil prices had reached a level of 123 dollars per barrel. There is no 
justification for refusing to make a substantial cut in the prices of 
petrol and diesel when the Government itself admitted that the 
administered prices of petrol and diesel are based upon an Indian basket 
calculated at 67 dollars a barrel. But the prices of aviation turbine 
fuel (ATF) has been brought down from around Rs.71,000 per kilo litre to 
around Rs.43,000 per kilo litre as of now. The ATF has also been exempted 
from import duty of 5 per cent. It is very unfortunate that the 
Government is providing such a largesse to the private airlines. Hence I 
urge upon the Government to reduce the prices of petrol and diesel and 
provide relief to the people who are suffering from all- round price rise 
of essential commodities. 
SHRI SAMAN PATHAK (West Bengal): Madam, I associate myself with this 
Special Mention.

SHRI SILVIUS CONDPAN (Assam): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
support this Bill which has been brought before this House by the 
Government to see that the jute farmers and jute production get the kind 
of attention that it deserves which, otherwise, is not getting from the 
Government so far. Sir, if I am not wrong, Assam -  in the North-Eastern 

417 
Region – is the next important jute producing State after West Bengal. I 
remember very well that earlier jute was very popularly cultivated by 
farmers. But, we have observed that gradually in our area the jute 
production has come down, because farmers have not got the real support 
price for their produce which they should  have  got.  And,  more  over, 
there is no organisation to look after various issues pertaining to  

418 
jute, except the Jute Corporation of India. Sir, Jute Corporation of 
India is only interested in buying jute and has its own marketing. The 
jute farmers are totally deprived of everything. As a result of this, 
slowly, the jute production in Assam and its neighbouring areas in the 
North-Eastern Region has come down. The farmers are not getting 
incentives from the Government, either from the State or the Central 
Government. Now, I am very happy to say that the Government has brought 
forward this Bill which contains far- reaching measures to safeguard the 
interests of farmers, also increase the production of jute and, thereby, 
bring jute production on the industrial map of the country. I f it is not 
on the industrial map of India, at least, jute industry will come on to 
the surface again, Sir, senior Member who spoke before me from the other 
side has said that there should be protection to jute growers in this 
Bill. In this Bill, except certain nominal mention of giving 
representation to jute producing farmers, there is no other mention in 
the proposed Bill that the jute farmers will get adequate protection from 
the Government, both from the Central and the State. Now, I do not see 
any co- ordination mechanism in the proposed Bill between the State 
Governments and the Jute Body. So, I draw the attention of the hon. 
Minister and request him to see that there should be striking provisions 
in the Bill with regard to duties of the jute growing States, co-
ordination with farmers with that of the policy of the Central Government 
so that, principally, the jute-growers as the tea planters get sufficient 
attention from the Government, both at the Centre as well as the States – 
who are equally important cash- crop-producers also get the same 
attention. If they would get due attention, they would definitely produce 
quality jute, and only then the intention of the Government, through this 
Bill, to constitute the Jute Board of India will really be fruitful, 
otherwise the Board will remain only in the namesake. Provisions have 
been made in the Act to protect the jute farmers, to enhance their 
production and to enhance the quality production. Likewise, many other 
encouraging things have been mentioned in this Act. It is very 
encouraging to go through it. But as my former speaker has expressed his 
apprehensions about the constitution of the Board, it does not 
sufficiently mention that there would be adequate representation of 
farmers in the Board. I would also like to draw the attention of the 
Government to see that some arrangement is made so that the jute farmers 
get due protection. In my State, I have experienced that the jute farmers 
agitate against the State Government, but the State Government has no 
jurisdiction to assure them a support price. So, the farmers commit 
suicide. Now, they have abandoned the production of jute in that area. 
During the British regime, in our early childhood days, we had seen that 

419 
abundant quantity of jute would be produced in Assam because the valley 
area of Assam was very much congenial to production of jute and paddy. It 
was known as the granary of both, jute and rice. But, now, the jute has 
almost disappeared. It has become a small commodity of production. But 
there used to be a large quantity of production, next to West Bengal. 
That's why I am grateful to the Government for bringing forward this 
piece of legislation. Now, hopefully, this area is going to be paid due 
attention. But I am only expressing my concern and drawing the attention 
of the hon. Minister that there is nothing very clearly mentioned about 
the role of State Government to make this Board effective. It is also 
mentioned that the Board will remain in Kolkota. I don't want to dispute 
that. I am happy that it is nearer to Assam. But the agencies, which will 
be spread out in different jute- producing areas, also need to be 
empowered so that they may protect the interests of the jute farmers. 
They will regulate the jute market. They will also have a role in 
deciding the support price for jute farmers. Jute is much more important 
than other agricultural  crops  because  it is a cash crop. But this cash 
crop has gone  

420 
out of scenario. It is very alarming because, this being a cash crop, the 
industry was also bringing in a lot of revenue to the Government; and, 
the States, where it was being grown, were also earning a good revenue. 
Farmers were also becoming economically better. Still the farmers would 
like to grow more and more jute, as compared to other crops, if they get 
due protection. And, with this Bill – when they would come to know that 
they were going to have some legal protection for jute growing, for 
promoting quality jute they will be given technical know- how by the 
Government – they will be earning a lot more than by growing other crops. 
I am really very happy to go through this Bill. I support this Bill. Once 
this Bill is passed, the Government will be doing an immensely good job 
for the welfare of the jute farmers, for the promotion of the jute 
industry. And, thus, we will be able to enhance the State economy and the 
Central economy by promoting the interests of the jute growers, and 
thereby, the jute industry. With these words, I support this Bill. I 
conclude, Sir.

SHRI MOINUL HASSAN (West Bengal): Sir, so far as the National Jute 
Board Bill, 2008, is concerned, it is a welcome step by the Government of 
India. There are many organisations for the development of jute and jute-
allied sectors, namely, the National Centre for Jute Diversification; the 
Jute Manufacturers' Development Council; and, two or three smaller 
organisations also. Now all of it is transferred to the National Jute 
Board and is under one umbrella. The different organisations now lapse 
and the new one is coming out. 
Firstly, in 2006, this Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha and now it 
is before Rajya Sabha. Sir, jute is an important product of our country, 
which is earning foreign exchange. As far as the world exports are 
concerned, our share is 43 per cent according to the figures of 2006, 
and, it is increasing day by day. It is an eco-friendly product and it is 
a cash crop. Lakhs of farmers depend on this only product. 
I must say that it is a welcome step but I have some critical 
observations to make so far as the Bill is concerned. 
Sir, the constitution of the board has been well discussed. Before 
going to this, Chapter 2, I would like to mention about the permanent 
office of the Board. It mentions that the permanent office of the Board 
shall be at Kolkata, State of West Bengal. There is no problem because 
West Bengal is a big jute growing State. But it is further written, "or 
such other place..." 
I find no reason as to why such clause has been incorporated meaning 
thereby that the Government of India may by notification change the 
office. I must say that this is not fair. 
So far as the Members of the Board are concerned, there shall be 21 
Members and one is to be nominated as the Chairman, and, most of the 
Members are nominated. Two- three points raised by the previous speaker 
about the representation of farmers are well taken. Why do you have only 
3 members? I am also of the opinion that there are only six, seven jute 
growing States in the country. Why can't these seven become the Members? 

435 
If it is not possible, there is a second option in this regard. Maybe one 
is permanent member, and, that is, West Bengal, and, others are to come 
on a rotational basis. If, in this scenario, it is not possible that 
other Members may become the permanent members, they can become 'invitee 
members'. 
Sir, a discussion should take place on the development of jute sector 
of our country. There is one more thing, which I would like to say and 
that is about the representation of officials of the State Government. 
What is the method in this regard? At page 3, first line, it is written, 
"three members to be  nominated  by  the  Central  Government  by  
notification  in  the  alphabetical order..." As far as I  

436 
know, it means the alphabetical order of the States. Andhra Pradesh will 
come first, followed by Assam, Bihar, Meghalaya, Orissa, Tripura and then 
the State of West Bengal will come in the last. I have no objection. But 
the State of West Bengal, which is a big State and which grows jute in a 
big way, will come in the last. I suppose it is hot a good method to 
choose the officials from the State Governments. 
There is another criticism. So far as the Board is concerned, most of 
the people are coming by way of nomination. With regard to the 
representation of workers, farmers or three Members of Parliament –  two 
from the Lower House and one from the Upper House the people – even then, 
it is only 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 who can talk about jute- growers and the workers 
etc. This is so far as Board is concerned. 
My second point is about the functions. There is a mention of 21 
functions. But I would like to say that we should emphasise on the micro-
level diversifying unit, which belongs to the self- help groups. Most of 
the women are the members in these self- help groups. They are engaged in 
a big way so far as diversification of jute products is concerned. In my 
opinion, function or activity of the Board must confine to this area. In 
this regard I would like to say that training programmes should be there. 
If we are very much eager or we are intending to diversify the jute 
product, training is very necessary. But today, there is inadequacy of 
training. There is a huge demand outside our country. But, if there is no 
sufficient training, we are not in a position to go, in a big way, to 
diversify our products. In this regard, I would like to say that the 
training portion should be strengthened in the National Jute Board. 
We have come to know and it is decided by the Government of India to 
establish jute parks in different parts of the country. May I know from 
the hon. Minister what is the present status of jute parks? In our State 
of West Bengal, there are three jute parks ready to take off. At least, 
two jute parks are in a position to take off. But, what is the outline of 
these jute parks? What will happen in these jute parks? We have some 
experience in Rajasthan. One private jute park is there in Rajasthan. It 
may be there in Gujarat or in some other part of the country. But, in a 
jute-growing State like West Bengal, Assam, Bihar, Orissa or Tripura, we 
have no jute park. 
[The Vice-Chairman (SHRIMATI JAYANTHI NATARAJAN) in the Chair] 
So, there should be a comprehensive outline provided to this. I would 
like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister that we should draw an 
exhaustive plan regarding jute parks under the Textile Ministry. It is a 
fact that jute growers are the worst sufferer farmers in this country. 

437 
They are not getting the minimum support price. In my State there are 
around 40 lakh jute growers. Every time they face a crisis, they are the 
first to sell their products in distress. We should do something for 
these jute growers. 
Again, I would like to mention that jute workers' strike is going on 
since 1st December. Jute mills are closed. The Government is in a 
position to interfere, specially the Government of India. 
My last point, Madam, is, about role of the JCI. My colleague, Mr. 
Mohammed Amin has already mentioned about this. I would like to say that 
the JCI is a failed institution. It never comes into  
the  picture  in  the  market  when jute is in the hands of the jute 
growers. When jute is in the hands of  

438 
3.00 P.M. 
middlemen, the JCI will come into the picture in the market or in the 
mandi. So, I am in a position to say that it is a failed organisation. We 
must revamp the entire organisation. I would like to say that this is a 
welcome step. I congratulate the Textile Minister. Thank you.

The Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament (Amendment) Bill, 
2008. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS AND THE 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY): 

451 
Madam, thank you for giving me this unique opportunity to move this Bill 
for the consideration of the House. Madam, I beg to move: 
That the Bill further to amend the Salaries and Allowances of Officers 
of Parliament Act, 1953, as passed by Lok Sabha, be taken into 
consideration. 

452 
Madam, with the adoption of the recommendations of the Sixth Central 
Pay Commission by the Government of India effective from 1st January, 
2006, the salaries of the Secretaries to the Government of India and that 
of the Cabinet Secretary have been raised to Rs.80,000 and Rs.90,000 
respectively. The Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament 
had been revised by the Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of 
Parliament (Amendment) Act, 2006 with effect from 15th September, 2006 
and by amendment of the rules with effect from 12th December, 2006. 
Keeping this in view and to maintain parity, between the salary of the 
President, the Chairman of Council of States and the Governors of the 
States, it is proposed to consider and pass the Salaries and Allowances 
of Officers of Parliament (Amendment) Bill, 2008 further to amend the 
Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Parliament Act, 1953, as passed by 
Lok Sabha, to provide that the Chairman of the Council of States shall be 
entitled to an enhanced salary of Rs. 1,25,000 per mensem. 
The above provision would involve a recurring expenditure from the 
Consolidated Fund of India to the tune of Rs. 10,22,000 per annum. 
Madam, the Bill is very simple and non- controversial in nature. Based 
on the recommendations of the Sixth Pay Commission that have enhanced the 
salaries of the Government officers and keeping in view the salary of the 
President of India which has been enhanced, this Bill has been brought in 
this House. The Lok Sabha has already passed this Bill. Therefore, I 
commend this Bill for consideration by the House. Whether it has to be 
passed without discussion or with discussion, it has to be decided by the 
House. 
The question was proposed.

is the Ethics Committee; there are guidelines drawn out to the effect 
that we have to declare in writing that there will not be conflict of 
interest, and all that. Members of Parliament are basically 100 per cent, 
24 x 7, all- time Members of Parliament. When such is the case with 
Members of Parliament, you should take care of them too. That is my 
submission. And I would like to support this Bill which proposes to 
increase the Chairman's salary from Rs.40,000 to Rs. 1,25,000. 
DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Madam, I support the 
Salaries and Allowances of Officers of Members of Parliament (Amendment) 
Bill, 2008. The post, which is adorned by the individual, actually 
carries a lot of weight in the international arena too. It is not a post 
on the basis of salary alone, but it is a post which carries a lot of 
work also. 
As Shri Ahluwalia has correctly mentioned, Members of Parliament are 

455 
now doing a lot of job. At the same time, we are portrayed in newspapers 
and media as if we only get adjournments made every day and stop working, 
and we are jolly well enjoying the holidays. That is the feeling which 
the people are getting about the Members of Parliament. Therefore, 
whenever we go out to address any public meeting or the University 
students, etc., we explain to them, "This is the general thinking about 
the Members of Parliament. But think of our work in Committees. We have 
Standing Committees and other Parliamentary Committees where we are doing 
a lot of research work; we have to do a lot of reading and discuss with 
people several things. After intense discussions and analysis, we come 
out with the best report possible, by putting all the wise decisions 
which have been given by different people. This work is carried out for 
more than 100 days a year." Therefore, we have to also show to the public 
how we are working. Recently, in a meeting with the IAS Academy,  I  had  
an  opportunity  to raise this subject with them. There were IAS officers 
of 10 years'  

456 
experience and also raw people who were just probationers. About 300 
officers were sitting there. I asked whether anyone of them can say 
something about the Parliamentary Standing Committees. None of the 
officers raised his hand. Only one new- comer, a probationer told that 
there is a Committee by which you can monitor the work of the Executive. 
That was the answer he could give. First of all, we have to market 
ourselves. How, we, as the Members of Parliament, are doing the work. We 
have to say to the people just like the Europe and America are saying. In 
Europe and America, they are telling it through a plenary session. They 
call it a plenary session. Even in U.K., I could find out that in the 
morning session, they are sitting as a Committee, and in the afternoon, 
they are sitting as a plenary session. Therefore, we have to tell the 
people that how we are working; otherwise, even this small amount of 
Rs.15,000 per month, which we are getting as a salary –  somebody said 
that it is equal to the salary of a Class IV or the lowest cadre employee 
– they feel that it is too much taxing on the people. 
In the same way, Madam, I feel that the Chairmanship of the Council of  
States is a very, very important post. It is so because it holds both the 
administrative work and also the work relating to presiding over meetings 
of the Council of States, meeting the dignitaries, going on foreign tours 
and also discussing certain issues which are very much relevant now. I 
feel that even this amount of Rs. 1,25,000 is not sufficient. I am saying 
this because when you are fitting in the topmost 1,2 and 3, then it 
should be commensurate not only with buildings and paraphernalia but also 
with emoluments that they are getting. That also speaks about it. We need 
not compare it with the President of the United States or the Prime 
Minister of the U.K. or any other country. We put it in the Constitution 
saying that Rs.1 lakh or Rs.50,000 will be the salary of the President of 
India. That shows that that was the topmost figure at that time. But, now 
the CEO of a company is earning Rs.5 crores per year or Rs.10 crores per 
year. Therefore, we have to increase the value of that particular post by 
giving more emoluments because they are doing a wonderful job of 
coordinating with the people and giving a stature to the country. 
Whenever we mention the President or the Vice- President, who holds the 
Chairmanship of the Council of States or the Speaker or the Prime 
Minister or the Ministers, they hold certain dignity. We have to give 
them more perquisites in financial terms. They should be given more for 

457 
that. But, at the same time, we have to see that they accountable, they 
are beyond all doubts of corruption and other practices, influences and 
other things. These aspects we have to bring to the knowledge of the 
people and more so to the knowledge of the media. It is not that 
politicians have to come with bare hands and work throughout the year. 
They are accountable for that. They should also be paid for that. 
Therefore, that sort of thinking has to be developed in the minds of the 
people. 
Madam, regarding the administrative side, I would like to comment upon 
it and it may not be out of context to mention here. The Chairman of the 
Council of States has the right to nominate the Vice- Chancellors of the 
Central Universities, the deemed universities and certain other posts. 
When the Chairman takes a decision, that has to be followed as it is. It 
should not simply go from one Department to another Department and 
another Department and wait for one year. I can give a  

458 
straight example concerning my State. It is relating to the Gandhi Gram 
University, which is a prestigious university. The post of the Vice-
Chancellor is lying vacant for the past one year. It was already cleared 
by the Chairman of the Council of the States, but it is not finding the 
light of the day. Why? It is so because it goes through many Departments. 
These Departments are coming forward and putting many questions. There 
should be proper consultation between various Departments before a 
decision is taken. The necessary papers should be built up before taking 
a decision. And once a decision is taken, then, everything should be 
obeyed. Madam, I could cite one example here. Wh en I visited China with 
the blessings of Madam Sonia Gandhi I had discussions with the top- level 
people there. What they say is, even if the Chairman of a municipal 
corporation takes a decision, that would be followed by the topmost 
person in China. When the topmost person takes a decision, nobody will 
question it; the next day it will be acted upon by everybody. But, here, 
if you take a decision, it will take its own course. What is the purpose 
in having a position or name like this? If the person has decided it, it 
should be acted upon immediately; it has to be respected, and weightage 
should be given for that. 
With this, I fully support this, but we have to increase the salary of 
Members of Parliament, and perks and other things also because we people 
are working hard, 24 x 7, and we also should be paid for that; because we 
need to create substantial prestige in the eyes of the people, more so in 
the media. Thank you very much.

Committee, from the time to time, considers the issues relating to the 
Members of Parliament's salaries and allowances and other perks and it

decides. Therefore, we will take up the sentiments expressed by the hon. 
Members about the Members' salaries and allowances at the appropriate 
forum and see that the Members' issues are taken up in a proper manner.

of the Bill is that the officer or Member of Parliament means any of the 
following officers namely, Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of 
States and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the people. The 
general impression is that the officers of Members of Parliament apply to 
other officers of the Parliament. It only confines to the hon. Chairman, 
hon. Deputy Chairman, hon. Speaker and hon. Deputy Speaker only. The Bill 
is only confined to that. An issue raised by the hon. Member, Shrimati 
Brinda Karat about the staff. I have appreciation for all the officers of 
Rajya Sabha who are working here right from the Secretary General to the 
other officers. They are doing commendable job and they have been helping 
the Members of Parliament in functioning. I can see that if any Member 
who gives a notice, with in minutes the notice is being forwarded and 
action is being taken and they are working with a great sense of duty. We 
have no doubt about it. But, Sir, the hon. Chairman is the deciding 
authority for the facilities and perks of the officers of Rajya Sabha.

Chairman will decide on it. Sir, since the hon. Members have given their 
unanimous support to this Bill without any reservation, I request the 
House to return this Bill. Hon. Members have also mentioned about the 
issue of salaries and allowances for Members of Parliament. We will tak e

Members of Parliament and apprise it that the salaries and allowances to 
Members of Parliament have to be increased on the lines of 
recommendations made by the Sixth Central Pay Commission. It was passed

in 2006. Now, we are in 2008. I will convey the feelings of the Members 
to the Chairman and the Committee. Then, the Committee will take 
appropriate decision.

DR. E.M. SUDARSANA NATCHIAPPAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, 
I fully support this Bill. The President of India represents the whole 
nation, and his or her tours to the foreign countries, national capital 
and other places of India very much represent the entire India. 
Therefore, when we are discussing his emoluments I feel that it has to be 
the highest one in our nation. Nobody aspires for this post on the basis 
of salary or emoluments. Everybody feels it the greatest opportunity to 
represent the whole nation and he is also the Commander- in-Chief of all 
the three Forces. Therefore, we have to create a big structure through 
various aspects not only for the protection of Rashtrapati Bhawan, but 
also for other facilities. It is the top- most post in India. With 
globalisation, salary reflects the quantum of work the person is doing or 

473 
that post holder is doing. We have to develop that type of thinking. When 
the Constitution was framed, we never thought of money and other aspects. 
I would like to quote the US President. He has a lot of restrictions 
along with benefits. I read in one newspaper that the elected President, 
Obama, wants to send his daughter ten days before to the White House to 
further her studies, but that was not allowed because they want to keep  

474 
the incumbent. It means that the person who is already in the office 
wants to be there till 14th January. That much of prestige they are 
giving to the President. Therefore, we have to give that reflection in 
the emoluments also. Instead of having these types of Bills on the basis 
of Pay Commission Report, I feel that that should be totally separate. It 
should be something, which should be considered in every three years or 
five years without following any Committee's or Commission's report. It 
is the prestige which we are giving to the Office; it is the prestige 
which we are giving to a particular individual. That type of attitude 
should be shown. I feel that it is high time for us to think about it. We 
need not debate this every time here and there and telling what are the 
reasons behind it. Now I come to aspects relating to office facilities, 
facilities after retirement and how he should be treated after 
retirement. Nowadays the President of India is becoming a very popular 
person also. Once it was a very confined Presidentship. But now he 
participates in mass rallies, mass meetings, addresses people and goes 
here and there. These types of things are happening. In one way, we 
should appreciate it. He is, however, the Constitutional head, but more 
popularity and focus is given to the Prime Minister. But, at the same 
time, we are focussing as a democratic head not as a monarchy. Therefore, 
I feel that these emoluments and, salaries which are fixed now are much 
less. I feel that it has to be enhanced and it has to be at par with the 
private sector where the Chief Executive is getting higher salaries. 
Similarly, all the Ministers and the Prime Minister should also get 
higher salaries. They are not coming for the job on the basis of salary 
but for the service that they are doing. They are doing it 24x7. 
Therefore, we have to treat them like that, not as a thing which is to be 
enhanced by way of debate. With this, I fully support all the three 
Bills.
